the_ledger_clause_under_review.quoted_text_verbatim_from_code: Tsai 1998, p.30 (restating/generalising NRS 1996): "Theorem 1. If a weak solution U of (1.3) belongs to L^q(R^3), for some q in (3,infinity], then it must be constant (and hence identically zero if q < infinity)."
the_ledger_clause_under_review.what_it_gates: fires (verdict EXCLUDED-BY-T1) whenever l3_norm_ladder()'s output converges -- and l3_norm_ladder() (lines 141-171) hardcodes the EXACT cube norm, i.e. q=3 precisely (variable names L3_cubed, cube ** (1.0/3.0); no other exponent appears anywhere in the function). There is no general-q L^q norm computed anywhere in this module -- the operational test is always, only, exactly q=3.

clause_by_clause_cross_check.verdict_on_the_cross_check: The ledger's OPERATIONAL test (q=3) correctly matches NRS 1996's actual hypothesis, per two independent obtainable sources agreeing exactly. The ledger's quoted DECIDING-CLAUSE TEXT (Tsai's Theorem 1, q in (3,infinity]) does NOT match NRS 1996's hypothesis -- it is a disjoint, non-overlapping range (open at exactly the value being tested), attributed by the ledger's own caption as 'restating/generalising NRS 1996' when in fact Tsai's Theorem 1 explicitly does NOT restate the q=3 case (already proved by NRS, not re-proved), and instead proves a new, harder, strictly-greater-than-3 case.

verdict_caveat: This is a citation/attribution discrepancy, not a computational or logical bug: the code's actual math (exact L3 convergence test) is correct and matches NRS 1996's real hypothesis per two independent obtainable sources, and the module's plain-English header (lines 64-68: 'u in L^3(R^3) forces u=0... Machine-read directly against THIS candidate's OWN l3_norm_ladder() result') already states this correctly without over-claiming Tsai's Theorem 1. The mismatch is localized to the deciding_clause TEXT leg 362 attached to the EXCLUDED-BY-T1 verdict (lines 534-539) and the identical header-comment quote (lines 364-367): both quote Tsai's Theorem 1 verbatim and caption it as restating NRS 1996, when the quoted range literally excludes the q=3 case being tested, and NRS 1996's own (separately, reliably attested) result is the theorem that actually covers that case.
